block.title: Battered fighter climbing toward distant light out of the abyss trench
block.positive: SNES-era 16-bit pixel art inspired concept rendering, bold dark outlines, saturated limited palette, vertical-climb composition in widescreen frame, subtle CRT scanline glow; ending scene painted at hi-resolution, wounded ascent, ultra-detailed large-format art with pixel-texture accents. Out of the throne trench, one slow climb at a time: a badly hurt steel-blue dart fighter angles upward across the frame from the lower left, its hull stripe burned away in a ragged band, one wingtip chipped, canopy cracked into a frost of fine fractures, cyan glass dim; the main engine lives as a single stretched flare of orange, the second sputters into a broken amber ribbon, and through the worst gash in its flank a faint interior light blinks once, mechanically, like a pulse that refuses to stop. Below and behind, the broken throne itself fills the bottom right of the frame — a shattered crown of black-blue reef-crystal and drowned fortress-mass, one enormous cracked ring of violet crystal split and tilted in the water where the seat of the deep tyrant used to be, its edges shedding a last slow rain of lilac shards into the trench; the biolume constellations that dusted the cliffs are going dark section by section from the bottom up, the abyss switching itself off now that its ruler is gone. Above: distance. The ceiling of the trench is far, far away, and through the gap in the spires a column of pale gold light comes down at an angle like something remembered from a different game — thin, physical, impossibly clean, illuminating drifting marine snow in a single lit stairway that ends exactly where the ship is pointing. The climb is not over in this frame; it is being refused to end. Palette of abyssal blues and violets dying out below, warm gold shaft above, one orange heart of engine fire in between, lifted deep-navy base, never pure black. No text, no letters, no UI.

Geometry must read: ship lower-left nose-up toward the shaft which enters upper-right-ish; if the shaft and ship don't point at each other, the entire "climb" premise dies. The one-blinking-flank-light is the survivor motif — flux.2 renders the damage vocabulary best here.
